claims.quote: The free-threaded build has additional overhead when executing Python code compared to the default GIL-enabled build.

claims.claim: Official Python documentation quantifies the single-threaded execution overhead of the free-threaded build as ranging from 1% to 8% depending on the hardware.

claims.quote: The changes to make CPython thread-safe without the GIL increase execution overhead for --disable-gil builds.
claims.claim: PEP 703 states that the internal changes required to make CPython thread-safe without the GIL inherently increase execution overhead.

claims.quote: For thread-safety reasons, an application running with multiple threads will only specialize a given bytecode once; this is why the overhead for programs that use multiple threads is larger compared to programs that only use one thread.
claims.claim: PEP 703 explains that multi-threaded programs have larger execution overhead than single-threaded ones due to bytecode specialization restrictions.

claims.quote: The largest contribution to execution overhead is biased reference counting followed by per-object locking.
claims.claim: PEP 703 identifies biased reference counting and per-object locking as the primary factors contributing to the execution overhead.

claims.quote: Note that this PEP would not affect the performance of the default (non --disable-gil) builds of CPython.
claims.claim: PEP 703 asserts that the performance impact is strictly isolated to the free-threaded build, and standard GIL-enabled builds will not be affected.

claims.quote: At this point we’re expecting a (worst case) performance penalty of 10-15%.
claims.claim: The Steering Council's acceptance of PEP 703 outlines an expected worst-case performance penalty of 10% to 15% for the free-threaded build.

claims.quote: The performance impact should be isolated to a free-threaded build; a GIL build should not see any performance impact in existing code.
claims.claim: The Steering Council mandates that any performance impact must be confined to the free-threaded build, ensuring existing GIL builds suffer no regressions.

claims.quote: The performance penalty on linear performance, comparing a free-threaded build against a with-GIL build, as measured by the pyperformance benchmarks (for example as run by Microsoft’s Faster CPython team, or Meta’s Python Runtime team), is currently around 10% (except on macOS, where it’s more like 3%).
claims.claim: PEP 779 reports that current single-threaded performance penalties hover around 10% on Linux/Windows and 3% on macOS.

claims.quote: Free-threaded Python currently sees about 15-20% higher memory use (geometric mean, as measured by pyperformance).
claims.claim: PEP 779 reports the memory use overhead of the free-threaded build to be approximately 15-20% higher than the with-GIL build.

claims.quote: We propose a target of 20% (geometric mean, as measured by pyperformance) for phase II.
claims.claim: PEP 779 proposes a hard target of a maximum 20% memory use overhead for the officially supported "Phase II" stage of free-threading.

claims.quote: we propose 15% as a hard performance target.
claims.claim: PEP 779 proposes a hard performance target allowing for a maximum 15% slowdown for the officially supported "Phase II" stage of free-threading.

claims.quote: Realistically, though, higher memory use is the cost of having efficient, safe free-threading, and we are unlikely to get this very close to the with-GIL build’s memory use without significant performance cost.
claims.claim: PEP 779 acknowledges that higher memory usage is an unavoidable cost for safe and efficient free-threading, and that minimizing it would significantly hurt CPU performance.
